However, their reliability in structural engineering computations—where validity is highly sensitive to implementation details—remains insufficiently quantified. This study evaluates four recent reasoning-oriented LLMs (Claude Sonnet 4.5, DeepSeekV3.2, GPT5, and Grok 4 Fastreasoning) under a unified API-based setup with default parameters and proposes a novel evaluation framework tailored for structural simulation. Five problems are designed to cover linear elasticity problems, forced vibration of a Timoshenko beam, and frame analysis. Solution strategies are constrained for comparability, and all generated codes are executed in a fixed Python environment with results verified against ABAQUS simulations or analytical solutions. The framework explicitly probes the importance of boundary conditions, selection of modeling assumptions, and implementation robustness. Common failure modes include incorrect treatment of traction-free boundaries, local-to-global transformation errors due to inconsistent local-axis definitions, and numerical instability induced by the choices of ways to impose boundary conditions. Overall reliability shows GPT‐5 is best model among those models tested. {"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=quantitative+benchmarks+and+metrics+for+evaluating+autonomous+scientific+problem+formulation+and+agenda+setting&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.36227/techrxiv.177162480.04513202/v2\", \"title\": [\"Evaluating Agentic Artificial Intelligence: A Comprehensive Survey of Metrics, Benchmarks, and Methodologies\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>Agentic Artificial Intelligence (Agentic AI) refers to autonomous systems capable of multi-step planning, subgoal generation, tool use, adaptation, and sustained decisionmaking. As such systems are increasingly deployed in robotics, scientific discovery, software engineering, and large language model (LLM)-based agents, the need for rigorous and multidimensional evaluation has become critical. However, existing evaluation practices, largely inherited from supervised learning and short-horizon reinforcement learning, fail to capture essential agentic properties such as long-horizon coherence, robustness under uncertainty, autonomy, safety, and adaptive behavior. This survey presents a structured and comprehensive analysis of evaluation methodologies for Agentic AI. We introduce an elevendimensional taxonomy encompassing task success, output quality, planning and reasoning, decision-making under uncertainty, tooluse effectiveness, autonomy and human intervention, learning and adaptation, safety and alignment, efficiency and resource utilization, multi-agent collaboration, and long-term memory consistency. Using this taxonomy, we systematically examine the growing ecosystem of benchmarks, frameworks, and evaluation tools, highlighting how they assess agent interactions, behavioral trajectories, and long-horizon performance across reinforcement learning agents, LLM-based agents, and multi-agent systems. Building on this analysis, we identify persistent evaluation gaps, including non-determinism, limited reproducibility, benchmark overfitting, incomplete safety assessment, and insufficient longhorizon evaluation. We conclude by outlining future research directions toward standardized, interpretable, and reliabilityfocused evaluation frameworks that more accurately reflect the real-world capabilities, limitations, and risks of Agentic AI.</jats:p>\",…

Title:
Fully Decentralized Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning with Networked Agents
Authors:
Kaiqing Zhang
,

Abstract:
We consider the problem of \emph{fully decentralized} multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), where the agents are located at the nodes of a time-varying communication network. Specifically, we assume that the reward functions of the agents might correspond to different tasks, and are only known to the corresponding agent. Moreover, each agent makes individual decisions based on both the information observed locally and the messages received from its neighbors over the network. Within this setting, the collective goal of the agents is to maximize the globally averaged return over the network through exchanging information with their neighbors. To this end, we propose two decentralized actor-critic algorithms with function approximation, which are applicable to large-scale MARL problems where both the number of states and the number of agents are massively large. Under the decentralized structure, the actor step is performed individually by each agent with no need to infer the policies of others. For the critic step, we propose a consensus update via communication over the network. Our algorithms are fully incremental and can be implemented in an online fashion. Convergence analyses of the algorithms are provided when the value functions are approximated within the class of linear functions. Extensive simulation results with both linear and nonlinear function approximations are presented to validate the proposed algorithms. Our work appears to be the first study of fully decentralized MARL algorithms for networked agents with function approximation, with provable convergence guarantees.
